prime.problem: A reasoning model decides for itself when to stop thinking. It sometimes stops early on a wrong answer, and you have no exact way to make it think longer or shorter. Asking in the prompt doesn't work because the model can't count its own tokens.
prime.fits: Builds on chain of thought and test-time compute: spending more tokens at inference can buy accuracy. s1 is the simplest version of that idea, with one sequential trace whose length is controlled from outside, on a model fine-tuned on only 1,000 examples.
expect: thinking tokens and the end-of-thinking marker
budget forcing (force the stop / block it and append “Wait”)
s1K: picking 1,000 examples by quality, difficulty and diversity
the scaling curve and where it flattens
prime.goal: Explain how blocking one token makes a model re-check its answer, read the paper's scaling curve and say where and why it flattens, and argue why this works only on a model that has already learned to reason.

attend: Why does editing the decoding loop give exact control over thinking length when a length instruction in the prompt doesn't?
What makes the model treat an appended “Wait” as a cue to re-check, and why did “Hmm” and “Alternatively” do worse?
Which of the three s1K filters does the most work, and what does the 59K-vs-1K result say about data quantity?
Why does accuracy stop rising after four “Wait”s instead of climbing forever?
How much of s1-32B's ability comes from the teacher model's traces rather than from budget forcing?

must: The model ends thinking by emitting an end-of-thinking token → budget forcing controls that one token from outside → insert it to cut thinking short, block it and append “Wait” to stretch it → exact control with no retraining (100% control vs 40% for a length instruction in the prompt)

Training traces often say “Wait” before a re-check → after fine-tuning, the model continues an appended “Wait” by re-reading its work → it can catch a slip (raspberry: 2 → 3) → AIME24 50.0% → 53.3% (×2) → 56.7% (×4)

Extra thinking only re-uses what the model already knows → after a few re-checks there is nothing new to find, and blocking the stop more often causes repetitive loops → the curve is flat from ×4 to ×6, and the context window sets a hard cap

Picking hard, varied, clean questions matters more than quantity → s1K (1,000) scores 50.0% vs 53.3% for all 59K at 56× less training compute, while random or longest-only sets of 1,000 score 26.7–36.7% → a short fine-tune switches on reasoning the pretrained model already has
elevated: The traces were distilled from Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking → the habit of re-checking was copied from a stronger reasoner → s1.1, trained on DeepSeek-R1 traces, reaches 56.7% with no forcing, so the teacher matters as much as the “Wait”s
AIME24 has 30 problems → each one is 3.3 points → the whole budget-forcing gain (50.0 → 56.7) is two problems, so small differences between methods are noisy
reference: Pool: 59,029 questions from 16 sources → 51,581 after the quality filters → 24,496 after the difficulty filter (drop anything Qwen2.5-7B or 32B solves) → 1,000 across 50 domains
Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: 5 epochs, 315 steps, 26 minutes on 16 H100s (7 GPU-hours); 59K took 394 GPU-hours
Only 53.6% of s1K traces reach the right answer; the wrong ones were kept on purpose

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences how s1 gets a model to think longer and why the gain stops. Or redraw the raspberry sketch and mark where budget forcing acts.
checklist: fine-tune on 1,000 hard, varied traces from a stronger model
the model signals the end of thinking with one special token
force that token to stop early; block it and append “Wait” to continue
the model re-checks and sometimes fixes its answer
gains flatten after a few “Wait”s (loops, nothing new to check) and the context window caps it

retrieve.q: Explain why a budget written into the prompt (“think for up to 2,048 tokens”) gives poor control while budget forcing gives exact control.
answer: the model can't count its own tokens, so it overshoots the requested length
budget forcing acts on the decoder, not on the model's judgement
the end-of-thinking token is inserted or blocked by code, so the limit holds every time

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens, token by token, when s1-32B tries to end its thinking and you want it to think more.
answer: the model's most likely next token is the end-of-thinking marker
the decoder drops that token and appends the text “Wait”
the model continues from “Wait” as if it chose it, usually re-reading its work
repeat N times, then let it stop and write the answer

retrieve.q: You have a fixed inference budget for a maths product. Argue when you would spend it on more “Wait”s for one trace, and when on several shorter traces with a vote.
answer: “Wait” helps until the knee (×4 in the paper), and is cheap to add
past the knee it adds tokens and latency with no gain, and can loop
one trace is capped by the context window; parallel traces aren't
the paper's Figure 7: search or voting over parallel traces kept scaling past where one sequential trace stopped

compare.q: Snell et al. spend test-time compute on search and revision; s1 spends it on one longer trace. What is fundamentally different, and when would you pick each?
answer: s1 is purely sequential: one trace stretched by “Wait”
search samples many candidates and needs a verifier or reward model
sequential reuses earlier reasoning but flattens and hits the context limit
pick search when you have a good verifier and parallel hardware; pick budget forcing when you want a simple, exact dial

compare.q: R1-Zero learned to re-check through RL; s1 copies re-checking from distilled traces and triggers it with “Wait”. Which one creates the habit, and how does each fail?
answer: RL creates the behaviour from reward; s1 imitates a teacher that already had it
s1 is capped by its teacher and its training traces (only 53.6% correct)
RL is costly and unstable but can go past the teacher (r1 79.8% vs s1-32B 56.7% on AIME24)
budget forcing can sit on top of an RL model too, which the paper lists as future work

predict.q: Take the original Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, with no s1K fine-tuning, and append “Wait” every time it tries to stop. Would you expect it to gain as much as s1-32B did? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Probably not. The base model never learned that “Wait” starts a re-check, and it doesn't use the think/answer markers that budget forcing acts on. The paper only applies budget forcing to fine-tuned s1 models. Its explanation (§6.1) is that the fine-tune switches on reasoning from pretraining and “Wait” then extends it. Without that switch there is little to extend. This is an inference from the paper, not a result it reports.

apply.task: Using Table 5 (s1-32B on AIME24: no forcing 50.0%, “Wait” ×1 53.3%, ×2 53.3%, ×4 56.7%) and the fact that AIME24 has 30 problems, convert each score to problems solved. Then write a one-paragraph recommendation for how many “Wait”s to ship, noting how much of the evidence is one problem's worth.
apply.done: You have 15, 16, 16 and 17 problems, you name ×4 as the best measured setting, and you say the gain between settings is one problem each time, so it needs a bigger test set to trust.
